unitOverview: Evaluation means looking carefully at a source and deciding how much you can trust it and how useful it is. You do this by finding out who made it and why, sorting what it says into facts and opinions, naming its strengths and limitations, and then saying what you think about it, with a clear reason.

explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Evaluation
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown two of the six thinking skills this year. In Research you learned to find out about a topic in a careful, tidy way. In Analysis you learned to look closely at a topic and ask why things happen. Now you are ready for the third skill: Evaluation.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

In Research you gathered sources. But not every source is worth trusting. Some are helpful, some are out of date, and some are only trying to sell you something. Evaluation is the skill of weighing a source, so you know how much of it to believe. Think of it like choosing fruit at the market. You do not put every mango in your basket without checking it first. You look each one over, and keep the good ones. Evaluation teaches you to do the very same thing with information.

Why does this matter beyond school? Every day, grown-ups are told all kinds of things: by adverts, by the radio, by people selling something. A parent deciding whether a health product really works. A shopper checking if a bargain is real. A whole family deciding whether to believe a rumour. All of them need to judge who and what to trust. A learner who practises evaluation now will be much harder to fool, for the rest of their life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way.
Analysis — looking closely at a topic and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how useful, trustworthy or strong a source really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you change your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our way, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. Evaluation especially loves a good discussion, because talking through a source out loud helps you spot what is strong about it and what is weak. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it like a real conversation.

Your evaluation skill will grow in three stages this year, just as it did for Research and Analysis. You will begin by starting each skill, then move on to developing it, and finally get better at it. Do not worry if judging a source feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', talk to your tutor as if it were a friendly study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It will discuss your ideas, disagree with you kindly, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best work, ask the questions that matter most, and hear how other learners judged the same sources.

explainers.title: Meet Hodan, our evaluator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each skill clear, we will follow one Year 5 learner all the way through the unit. Her name is Hodan, and she is a student at Ehel Academy in Burao.

One evening, Hodan walks through the market with her mother. At a busy stall, a bright hand-painted sign catches her eye: Malaria-Gone Lotion — one rub and mosquitoes never bite you again! The seller calls out that families everywhere trust it. Hodan thinks of the mosquito net hanging over her bed at home, the one her family uses every single night. She wonders: if this lotion really works so well, do we even need the net any more? And should people believe everything a seller shouts across a market?

That question becomes Hodan's whole project for this unit. To answer it fairly, she cannot just trust her first feeling. She has to gather sources about malaria and about the lotion, and work out which ones are useful, who made them, why they made them, and what she truly thinks. In other words, she has to evaluate. As you meet each new skill, you will see exactly what Hodan does with it, and you will do the same with a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through this unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. A Challenge is a topic that matters both in the wider world and right where you live. In this unit you will collect a small set of sources about your topic, evaluate each one, and use the best of them to say what you really think, just as Hodan will.

Here are four topics that come up again and again in the Horn of Africa, and that all need good evaluation. Any of these could become your Challenge:

Your classmates will care about different things. Hodan is drawn to the lotion and the mosquito net. Idris worries about the warning signs on the busy road near school. Sagal keeps hearing rumours about a vaccination day, and does not know what to believe. Faisal's older brother keeps getting adverts for 'easy money' phone deals. Any of these could grow into a strong Challenge.

You do not have to choose right now. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any source that makes you curious, or that gives you a little 'is that really true?' feeling. That feeling is an excellent sign of a good Challenge topic.
bullets: Health claims at the market — such as the Malaria-Gone Lotion, and whether it can really replace a mosquito net.
Road safety warnings — the signs and posters near a busy road, and whether people take real notice of them.
Rumours and real information about health days — such as a vaccination day at school, when rumours can spread fast.
Adverts for phone deals or 'easy money' — aimed at older brothers, sisters and parents.

explainers.title: So what is evaluation?
explainers.body:
In everyday life, to evaluate something means to decide how good or how useful it is. In Global Perspectives, evaluation means looking carefully at a source and deciding how much you can trust it and how useful it is. You do this by asking two simple questions about every source: who made it, and why did they make it?

Evaluation has three main parts, and this unit teaches all three:

Notice that evaluation is not about calling a source simply 'good' or 'bad'. It is more careful than that. A source can be excellent for one job and poor for another. A market seller's shout is a fine source if you want to know what is for sale, but a weak source if you want to know whether a lotion really stops mosquito bites. Evaluation is all about matching a source to your purpose.
bullets: Judging how useful a source is, by thinking about who made it and what its purpose was.
Weighing a source's strengths (what it is good at) and its limitations (what it cannot tell you).
Giving your own opinion about a source, pointing to what is in it and to the arguments it makes.

explainers.title: Skill 1: What is a source, and what is it for?
explainers.body:
A source is anywhere your information comes from: a leaflet, a poster, a website, a radio advert, or a person you talk to. Every source is made for a reason. That reason is called its purpose: what the maker was trying to do. Once you know a source's purpose, you understand it far better, because purpose changes how useful a source is and what it can be trusted for.

Here are some common purposes a source can have:
bullets: To explain how or why something happens, such as a health worker describing how malaria spreads.
To change your mind or persuade you, such as a market poster.
To describe what something is, such as a fact sheet about mosquitoes.
To sell you something, such as a lotion advert.
To give both sides fairly, such as a balanced radio programme.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Strengths and limitations of a source
explainers.body:
No source is perfect. Every source has strengths, the things it is good at, and limitations, the things it is not good at or cannot tell you. A skilled evaluator names both, instead of just saying 'I like it' or 'I do not like it'.

The trick is to think about what a source can and cannot give you. A source might be clear, or written by someone who knows the topic, or full of real examples: those are strengths. But the same source might be old, or show only one side, or never mention its own weak points: those are limitations.

explainers.title: Skill 3: How useful is a source for my goal?
explainers.body:
Now put purpose, strengths and limitations together to answer the big question: how useful is this source for what I am trying to do? A source is not useful or useless on its own. It is useful, or not, for a particular goal. So always ask: useful for what?

A simple way to check this is to finish two sentences for each source: it is useful because ..., and it is not so useful for .... When you can finish both, you have really evaluated the source.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Who made it? Thinking about the author
explainers.body:
The very first evaluation question is 'who?'. The person or group who made a source is called the author or creator. Knowing who made a source, and whether they really know the topic, tells you a great deal about how far to trust it.

When you meet a new source, ask yourself three quick things about its author:
bullets: Who made it — a named person, a health worker, a company, or nobody you can see?
What do they know — is health their job, or their subject, or are they just guessing?
Why did they make it — to help you understand, or to get something from you?

explainers.title: Skill 5: Fact or opinion?
explainers.body:
Sources are full of two different things, and a good evaluator can tell them apart. A factual claim is something that can be checked against real evidence. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.

Notice how differently they read:
bullets: Fact: A treated mosquito net stops most mosquitoes from biting you while you sleep. You could check this with a health worker.
Opinion: The lotion is the best protection you can buy. Someone could reasonably disagree.

explainers.title: Skill 6: The perspective of a source
explainers.body:
Everyone sees the world from their own point of view, and so does every source. This point of view is called a perspective. A source's perspective is shaped by who made it and what they want. Spotting the perspective of a source is a key part of evaluation, because it explains why a source says what it says.

A source is not wrong just because it has a perspective. Almost every source has one. The skill is to notice it, so you are not swept along without realising.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Can I trust it? Three quick tests
explainers.body: This is close to the heart of evaluation: deciding how far to trust a source. Three tests help you decide. Ask about expertise (does the maker really know the topic?), relevance (is it really about my question?), and bias (does it lean unfairly to one side?).
bullets: Expertise: a source made by someone who knows the topic, such as a nurse, is usually more trustworthy.
Relevance: a source is only useful if it is really about your question, not just near it.
Bias: a biased source leans one way on purpose, often because the maker has something to gain.

explainers.title: Skill 8: Comparing two sources
explainers.body:
When you have two or more sources about the same thing, it helps to line them up side by side and compare them. Ask what each one says, who made it, and how far you trust it.

Comparing shows you where sources agree and where they disagree. When two very different sources agree on something, that agreement is worth taking seriously. When they disagree, that is exactly where careful evaluation matters most.

explainers.title: Skill 9: Saying what you think - agree or disagree
explainers.body:
Evaluation is not only about sources. It is also about saying what you think of other people's perspectives. When you hear someone's view, you can agree, disagree, or land somewhere in between. The clever part is that agreeing is not all-or-nothing. You can sit anywhere on a line, from strongly agree to strongly disagree.

Here is the line you will use. When you hear a perspective, decide where you sit, and always give your reason:
bullets: Strongly agree — I think this is completely right.
Agree — I mostly think this is right.
Not sure — I can see both sides, or I need more information.
Disagree — I mostly think this is not right.
Strongly disagree — I think this is completely wrong.

explainers.title: Skill 10: Writing your own evaluation of a source
explainers.body: Now you bring every skill together to write your own evaluation of a single source. A written evaluation is a short piece where you weigh a source fairly and say what you think of it. Use this frame:
bullets: Who made it? Name the author or creator, and what they know.
What is it for? Say the purpose and the perspective.
Pick one point. Choose one clear thing the source says.
Comment on it. Use your own knowledge to give its strengths and limitations.
Give your view. Say whether you agree or disagree with the point, and why.

explainers.title: Staying safe when you check things online
explainers.body: Some of your sources for this unit will come from books, posters or people. Others might come from the internet, so a good evaluator also keeps themselves safe while they look. Staying safe is part of the skill, not an extra rule.
bullets: Never share your full name, home address, school or photos with strangers online.
If a page asks you to sign up, download something, or 'click to win', stop and check with a trusted adult.
If a page upsets or worries you, close it and tell your teacher or a grown-up at home.
Remember: a bright, exciting page is not automatically a true one. Slow down and evaluate it like any other source.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the evaluation cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every evaluation skill in this unit. Here is how they fit together into one smooth cycle you can use for any source:
bullets: Ask who made it, and why (the author and the purpose).
Sort what it says into facts and opinions.
Name its perspective.
Weigh its strengths and its limitations.
Test it for expertise, relevance and bias to decide how far to trust it.
Decide how useful it is for your goal.
Say what you think, agreeing or disagreeing, with a reason.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Reflection. Once you can evaluate sources and perspectives, reflection teaches you to turn that same careful, fair thinking on yourself: how you learn, how you change your mind, and what you will do better next time. Strong evaluation now will make strong reflection much easier later. Well done for growing a skill that will keep you wise for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a market stall, and the skill is what you take home from it.
We will use real topics such as health claims, road safety and rumours.
But the real prize is not to become an expert on malaria lotions. It is to become someone who can look at any source and decide, calmly, how far to trust it.

bigIdeas.title: The big questions an evaluator asks
lines: Who is the author or creator of this source?
What was their purpose, and what is their perspective?
What are the strengths and limitations of the source?
How useful and trustworthy is it for my goal, and what do I think?

bigIdeas.title: A source is not wrong just because it is trying to sell something
lines: A seller's poster can still contain some true facts, such as the price or where the stall is.
But when a maker has something to gain, such as a seller wanting to sell a lotion, check its biggest claims against a fairer source.
Being fair does not mean trusting nobody. It means noticing who gains, and weighing the source with care.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one topic that matters both in the world and where you live. This is your Challenge.
Good choices for this unit: health claims at the market, road safety warnings, rumours about a health day, or adverts for phone deals.
You will gather and judge sources about it, and by the end you will have written your own evaluation.

models.title: Evaluation happens at the market too
lines: Imagine a seller tells you their dates are the sweetest in Burao.
You do not just believe it at once. You ask yourself: does this seller really know, or are they just trying to make a sale?
Then your neighbour, who buys dates every week, says the same seller's dates really are the best. You trust your neighbour a little more, because she has nothing to gain by telling you.
Weighing the seller and your neighbour, and deciding who to trust, is real evaluation. You already do it.

So evaluation is not a strange, school-only activity. It is a calm, fair way of weighing what you are told, and you can get better and better at it. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, about sources that matter to your community.

models.title: Hodan matches her sources to their purpose
lines: A leaflet from Burao Health Clinic: its purpose is to explain how to stay safe from malaria.
A fact sheet on mosquitoes: its purpose is to describe how they spread disease.
An interview with a community health worker: its purpose is to share what she has seen in real homes.
The Malaria-Gone Lotion poster: its purpose is to make people want to buy the lotion.
A neighbour's story about never catching malaria: its purpose is to share one person's real experience.

See how knowing the purpose already tells Hodan a lot? The poster's purpose is to sell, so she will be careful before trusting its biggest claim. The clinic leaflet's purpose is to explain, so it may be fairer. Purpose is the first clue in every evaluation.

models.title: Hodan weighs the lotion poster
lines: A strength: it is bright, clear, and easy for anyone walking past to notice.
A limitation: it never explains how the lotion works, and it never mentions a mosquito net at all.
So the poster is useful for showing what the seller wants people to believe, but not for finding out the whole truth about staying safe from malaria. Naming both is the skill.

models.title: Hodan builds a useful-because table
lines: Hodan's goal: to find out whether her family really needs their mosquito net if they also use the lotion.
The clinic leaflet is useful because it explains what really protects against malaria; it is not so useful for showing what sellers say.
The fact sheet is useful because it gives clear, checked facts about mosquitoes; it is not so useful for suggesting what to do at home.
The lotion poster is useful because it shows how sellers try to persuade; it is not so useful for finding the real facts.

One more question makes evaluation really practical. Ask: which of my sources best helps me decide what to do? In Global Perspectives you gather information not just to know more, but to help make a good decision. The source that points to a clear answer is often the most useful of all.

models.title: Sagal checks who wrote two vaccination messages
lines: Sagal is worried about rumours before the school vaccination day. She finds two messages.
One is a leaflet from the health clinic, written by a named nurse, and dated this month.
The other is a voice message shared many times, with no name, saying the vaccination makes children ill.
Sagal trusts the clinic leaflet far more, because she can see who made it and that they really know the topic.

A message with no author is not always false, but it should make you careful. If you cannot tell who made something, or why, you cannot be sure it is fair. Always try to find the author before you rely on a source.

models.title: Hodan names the perspective of three sources
lines: The Malaria-Gone Lotion poster. Perspective: our lotion protects you, so buy it.
A leaflet from Burao Health Clinic. Perspective: a treated mosquito net is the best protection, every night.
A radio programme with a doctor and a market seller both speaking. Perspective: it tries to give both sides fairly.
Hodan can now see that the poster and the leaflet each push one way, while the radio programme tries to stay balanced.

models.title: Hodan sorts facts from opinions
lines: A fact sheet on malaria: mainly facts.
The lotion poster, 'trusted by families everywhere': mainly opinions and perspective dressed up as fact.
A report comparing net use in different towns: mainly facts.
A neighbour's story about never being bitten: mainly one person's experience and opinion.

Here is the clever part, and it surprises many learners. To persuade people well, you usually need both facts and opinions together. A fact on its own does not tell people what to do. An opinion on its own is not seen as good proof. But join them, and they become powerful: 'Treated nets stop most mosquito bites at night (fact), so I think every family should keep using one (opinion).' The fact gives the opinion its strength.

models.title: Hodan writes a short evaluation of the lotion poster
lines: Who made it: a market seller, whose job is to sell the lotion.
What it is for: to make people want to buy it; its perspective is that the lotion alone is enough protection.
A point: the poster says one rub means mosquitoes never bite you again.
Comment: a strength is that it is eye-catching and easy to notice; a limitation is that it never mentions how long the lotion lasts, or the mosquito net at all.
Hodan's view: I disagree that the lotion alone is enough, because the clinic leaflet and the fact sheet both say a treated net is the best protection, and the poster does not mention that at all.

That is a complete evaluation. Hodan named who made it and why, chose one point, weighed it with her own knowledge, and gave her honest view with a reason. When you can do this for a source of your own, you have truly learned to evaluate.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 3 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Evaluation.
Ask it: in one or two simple sentences, why is it useful to judge whether a source can be trusted?
Then tell your tutor about a time you saw an advert or heard a claim that you did not quite believe, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think evaluation means.
Ask it: is my idea missing anything important?
Then ask your tutor to give you one everyday example of evaluation that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source you have seen recently, such as a poster, a leaflet or a message.
Ask it to help you work out the purpose: was it made to explain, to persuade, to describe, or to sell?
Then ask: how might that purpose change how much I trust it?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one of your own sources to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you name one strength and one limitation of that source.
Then ask: for my goal, does the strength matter more, or the limitation?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your Challenge topic and your goal.
For one of your sources, finish the sentences: it is useful because, and it is not so useful for.
Then ask the tutor: which of my sources best helps me decide what to do?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one source to your AI tutor: who made it, and what you think they know about the topic.
Ask the tutor to help you decide how much the author makes you trust it.
Then ask: what is one thing I still do not know about who made this source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor two statements about your topic: one fact and one opinion.
Ask it to check that you have sorted them correctly.
Then ask the tutor to help you join a fact and an opinion into one persuasive sentence.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source with a clear point of view.
Ask it to help you say the source's perspective in one sentence, starting with the words: this source thinks.
Then ask: what might this source be leaving out because of its perspective?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one source to your AI tutor and run the three tests together: expertise, relevance and bias.
Ask it which of the three is the biggest problem for that source.
Then ask: what fairer source could I use to check this one?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your AI tutor two sources you have for your Challenge.
Ask it to help you find one thing they agree on, and one thing they disagree about.
Then ask: which of the two would I trust more, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to tell you a clear perspective on your topic, as if it were a classmate.
Say where you sit, from strongly agree to strongly disagree, and give your reason.
Then ask the tutor to argue the opposite view, and see whether it moves you.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Choose one source about your topic and tell your AI tutor about it.
Walk through the five steps together: who made it, what it is for, a point, its strengths and limitations, and your view.
Then ask the tutor to check that your evaluation is fair and gives a clear reason.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source you found online for your Challenge.
Ask it to help you check whether the page seems safe and trustworthy, not just exciting.
Then ask: what is one thing a trusted adult should know before I use this source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five matches to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then tell it the purpose of each of your own sources.
Ask the tutor: does knowing the purpose change how much I should trust each source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read your joined fact-and-opinion sentence.
Ask the tutor: is my sentence more persuasive with both the fact and the opinion together?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your table to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you have worked out each source's author and purpose correctly.
Then ask: which of my two sources should I trust more, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two strengths and two limitations to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you have been fair, or a little too kind or too harsh.
Then ask: for my goal, do this source's strengths outweigh its limitations?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your compare grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether it would trust the two sources the same way you did.
Then ask the tutor to help you improve the reason you found hardest to write.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you spotted how the poster uses bright words and pictures to persuade.
Then ask the tutor: what would a fairer source about this lotion look like?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor where you sit on the line and your two reasons.
Ask it to argue the opposite view as strongly as it can.
Then tell the tutor whether that moved you, and explain why you did or did not change your mind.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your topic, your message and your two supporting sources to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your sources really support your message, or only partly.
Then ask the tutor to help you make your reasons clearer and fairer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your finished evaluation to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you named both a strength and a limitation, and gave a clear reason.
Then ask the tutor to suggest one way to make your evaluation even fairer.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your quiz answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it which answer was your strongest, and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one evaluation skill to keep practising in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home about a claim or an advert they once believed, but later found out was not quite true.
Did it make them want to buy or do something? Did it tell the whole truth?
Bring their story, and your own ideas, to your next teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your compare grid of two sources and the one you trust more.
Share it in your next teacher session and compare how others judged their sources.

toolkit.title: The evaluation steps at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your source, good evaluation follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: Who and why: find the author and the purpose.
Fact or opinion: sort what it says.
Perspective: name the source's point of view.
Strengths and limitations: weigh what it is good at and not good at.
Trust: test it for expertise, relevance and bias.
Usefulness: decide how useful it is for your goal.
Your view: agree or disagree, with a reason.

toolkit.title: The Evaluation skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Evaluation means looking carefully at a source and deciding how much you can trust it and how useful it is. You do this by finding out who made it and why, sorting what it says into facts and opinions, naming its strengths and limitations, and then saying what you think about it, with a clear reason.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, never judge a source as simply 'good' or 'bad'; ask 'useful for what?'. Second, be fair: notice a source's perspective and weigh it with your eyes open, instead of believing it or throwing it away at once. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

You will use this skill far beyond Global Perspectives. Every time an advert, a message or even a friend tells you something, you can pause and quietly ask: who is telling me this, and why? That one small habit, practised often, will keep you thinking clearly for the rest of your life.

toolkit.title: A one-minute check for any source
toolkit.intro: When you do not have much time, run this fast version of the cycle. It catches most problems in under a minute, and you can do the full cycle later for your most important sources.
items: Who made it, and do they really know the topic?
Why did they make it: to help me, or to gain something?
Fact or opinion: is it something I could check, or just what they think?
Relevant: is it truly about my question, or only near it?
So what: how far will I trust it, and how will I use it?

toolkit.title: Your Stage 5 Evaluation learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your evaluation skill grows in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: A guide to the purpose of a source
toolkit.intro: Every source is made for a reason. Work out the purpose first, because it changes how useful a source is and how far to trust it. If the purpose is hard to spot, look at who made the source and what they might gain, because the purpose is usually hiding there.

rows: To explain
It shows how or why something happens.
A health worker explaining how malaria spreads.
To describe
It outlines what something is.
A fact sheet about mosquitoes.
To persuade
It tries to change your mind.
A leaflet urging families to use nets every night.
To sell
It wants you to buy something.
The Malaria-Gone Lotion poster.
To balance
It gives both sides fairly.
A radio programme with a doctor and a seller both speaking.

toolkit.title: Strengths and limitations, side by side
toolkit.intro: A strong evaluation always names both. Ask these questions about every source.
items: Is it clear and easy to understand?
Was it made by someone who knows the topic?
Does it give real examples or checked facts?
Is it closely about my question?
Is it out of date?
Does it show only one side?
Does the maker have something to gain?
Is it really about my question, or only near it?

toolkit.title: Who made it, why, and can I trust it?
toolkit.intro:
This is the core of evaluation. Ask 'who?' and 'why?', then run the three trust tests.

Remember: a source is not wrong just because it has a perspective or a bias. Notice who gains, then check its claims against a fairer source.

rows: Who made it?
Find the author or creator.
A named person, a health worker, a company, or nobody shown?
Why did they make it?
Find the purpose.
To help you understand, or to get something from you?
Expertise
Do they really know the topic?
Someone who knows the subject is usually more trustworthy.
Relevance
Is it really about my question?
A source can be interesting but off-topic.
Bias
Does it lean unfairly to one side?
A maker who gains, such as a seller, may be biased.

toolkit.title: Facts and opinions: a quick sorter
toolkit.intro:
Sort what a source says, then remember that to persuade you usually need both.

Opinion words such as best, worst, should, terrible or amazing are clues that you are reading an opinion, not a fact. When you spot one, slow down and ask whether the source can back it up.

rows: Fact
Can be checked and shown to be true.
A treated net stops most mosquito bites at night.
Opinion
What someone thinks; others may disagree.
This lotion is the best protection you can buy.
Perspective
A whole point of view, shaped by who made it.
Our lotion is all the protection you need.

toolkit.title: The agree and disagree line
toolkit.intro:
When you hear someone's perspective, decide where you sit, and always give a reason. You do not have to be all-or-nothing.

Sentence starters: 'I agree with ... because ...', 'I disagree with ... because ...', 'I can see why ... thinks that, but I ...'.

rows: Strongly agree
I think this is completely right.
Agree
I mostly think this is right.
Not sure
I can see both sides, or I need more information.
Disagree
I mostly think this is not right.
Strongly disagree
I think this is completely wrong.

toolkit.title: Frame: write your own evaluation
toolkit.intro:
Use this five-step frame to write a short, fair evaluation of any source. Aim for one short paragraph.

Sentence starters you can use: 'This source was made by ...', 'Its purpose is to ...', 'One point it makes is ...', 'A strength is ..., but a limitation is ...', 'I agree / disagree with this because ...'.
items: Who made it? Name the author and what they know.
What is it for? Give the purpose and the perspective.
Pick one point. Choose one clear thing the source says.
Comment on it. Use your knowledge to give its strengths and limitations.
Give your view. Say whether you agree or disagree, and why.

toolkit.title: One last thing to remember
toolkit.intro: Every good evaluator started exactly where you are now. You do not have to be perfect. You just have to be careful, honest and curious. If you get stuck, that is normal, and your AI tutor is ready to help you at any time.

checklists.title: Checklist: strengths and limitations
checklists.intro: A strong evaluation always names both. Ask these questions about every source.
items: Is it clear and easy to understand?
Was it made by someone who knows the topic?
Does it give real examples or checked facts?
Is it closely about my question?
Is it out of date?
Does it show only one side?
Does the maker have something to gain?
Is it really about my question, or only near it?

checklists.title: Checklist: can I trust this source?
checklists.intro: Run these three quick checks on any source before you lean on it. A quick way to test trust is to ask one thing: would the maker lose anything by telling the whole truth? If yes, such as a seller with something to sell, read the source with extra care.
items: Who made it, and do they really know the topic?
Why did they make it: to help me, or to sell me something?
Is it really about my question, or only near it?

challenge.intro: Look back at the four topics in the Lesson file (health claims at the market, road safety warnings, rumours about a health day, and adverts for phone deals). Choose one that matters to you, or think of your own. Then start a small collection of sources about it, because you cannot evaluate sources you do not have. Your sources do not need to be perfect. In fact, a mix of strong and weak sources makes this unit more interesting, because your whole job is to tell them apart.
topics: Write your chosen topic in one sentence: 'The topic I am working on is ...'.
Write one reason you care about it.
List three or four sources you could use, such as a leaflet, a poster, a website, or a person to ask.
checkpoints: The most useful source I found was ..., because ...
One source I decided not to trust was ..., because ...
After evaluating my sources, I now think that ...

activities.title: Match each source to its purpose
activities.label: Activity 2: Match each source to its purpose
activities.intro:
Every source is made for a purpose. Warm up by matching each source (1 to 5) to the purpose it was made for (A to E). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.

Then look at your own sources from your Challenge. Write the purpose of each one in a few words.
steps: A leaflet from Burao Health Clinic about mosquito nets.
A fact sheet describing how mosquitoes spread malaria.
A radio programme with a doctor and a seller both speaking.
An interview with a community health worker about her visits.
The Malaria-Gone Lotion poster at the market.
A. To describe what something is.
B. To explain how or why something happens.
C. To make you want to buy something.
D. To give both sides of an argument fairly.
E. To share one person's real experience.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five matches to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then tell it the purpose of each of your own sources.
Ask the tutor: does knowing the purpose change how much I should trust each source?

activities.title: Sort facts from opinions
activities.label: Activity 3: Sort facts from opinions
activities.intro: A fact can be checked and shown to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks, which others may disagree with. Sort each statement below into F for fact or O for opinion.
steps: A. A treated mosquito net stops most mosquitoes from biting you at night.
B. Malaria-Gone Lotion is the best protection you can buy.
C. Some mosquitoes are most active after sunset.
D. Everybody should throw away their old, torn nets.
E. Our clinic gave out 200 new nets this month.
F. Sleeping under a net feels much safer than using lotion alone.

boxes.title: A model: fact or opinion?
lines: A treated net stops most mosquitoes from biting you at night: this is a fact, because a health worker could check it.
Malaria-Gone Lotion is the best protection you can buy: this is an opinion, because it is what someone thinks and others could disagree.
Both sentences are about staying safe from mosquitoes. The difference is only whether they can be checked.

Then try the clever step from the Lesson: choose one fact and one opinion from your own topic, and join them into a single persuasive sentence, such as: 'Treated nets stop most mosquito bites at night, so I think every family should keep using one.'

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Then read your joined fact-and-opinion sentence.
Ask the tutor: is my sentence more persuasive with both the fact and the opinion together?

activities.title: Be a source detective: who made it, and why?
activities.label: Activity 4: Be a source detective: who made it, and why?
activities.intro:
Pick two of your sources. For each one, be a detective about the author and the purpose. Fill in a table like the one below.

If you cannot find who made a source, write 'no author shown'. That is an important finding, because a source with no author should make you more careful.

boxes.title: Two sources about staying safe from malaria
lines: Source 1: A leaflet from Burao Health Clinic, written by a named nurse, dated this month.
Source 2: A voice message shared many times, with no name and no date, that says the lotion works better than any net.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your table to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you have worked out each source's author and purpose correctly.
Then ask: which of my two sources should I trust more, and why?

activities.title: Weigh a source's strengths and limitations
activities.label: Activity 5: Weigh a source's strengths and limitations
activities.intro: Take one source you care about and weigh it properly. A strong evaluation always names both what a source is good at and what it cannot do, instead of just saying you like it or you do not.
steps: Name the source and who made it.
Write two strengths: things it is good at, such as clear facts, an author who knows the topic, or real examples.
Write two limitations: things it cannot do, such as being out of date, showing only one side, or not quite being about your question.
Finish this sentence: 'Overall, this source is useful for ..., but not for ...'.

boxes.title: A model: weighing the lotion poster
lines: A strength: it is bright, clear, and easy for anyone walking past to notice.
A limitation: it never explains how the lotion works, and it never mentions a mosquito net at all.
So the poster is useful for showing what the seller wants people to believe, but not for finding out the whole truth about staying safe from malaria. Naming both is the skill.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two strengths and two limitations to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you have been fair, or a little too kind or too harsh.
Then ask: for my goal, do this source's strengths outweigh its limitations?

activities.title: Compare two sources
activities.label: Activity 6: Compare two sources
activities.intro: Now compare two sources about the same topic. Line them up side by side, and decide which you trust more, and why.
steps: Write your goal in one sentence, such as 'I want to find out whether the lotion alone is enough protection.'
For each source, write what it says, and how far you trust it.
Write one thing the two sources agree on, if anything.
Write which source you would trust more, and give your reason.

boxes.title: A model: comparing two sources about the lotion
lines: Source 1: the clinic leaflet, written by a nurse, says a treated net is the best protection every night.
Source 2: the lotion poster, made by the seller, says one rub means mosquitoes never bite again.
What they agree on: mosquitoes can be dangerous, and it is worth protecting yourself.
What they disagree on: whether the lotion alone is enough, or whether you still need a net.
I trust the clinic leaflet more, because the nurse's job is to know about health, while the seller's job is to sell the lotion.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your compare grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether it would trust the two sources the same way you did.
Then ask the tutor to help you improve the reason you found hardest to write.

activities.title: Evaluate the lotion poster for bias
activities.label: Activity 7: Evaluate the lotion poster for bias
activities.intro: Adverts are made to sell, so they are a perfect test of evaluation. An advert is allowed to show only its best side, which is exactly why you must read it with care. Read the poster described below, then evaluate it for bias by answering the questions.
steps: Who made this poster, and what is their purpose?
What does the poster want you to feel about the lotion?
What true information does it leave out, and why?
Is this a fair source about staying safe from malaria? Explain your answer using the word bias.

boxes.title: The poster, described in words
lines: A bright hand-painted sign shows a smiling family with no mosquitoes near them.
The big words say: Malaria-Gone Lotion — one rub and mosquitoes never bite you again!
In tiny letters at the bottom it says: for outdoor use only, wash off before sleeping.
The poster hangs above a busy stall in the Burao market.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you spotted how the poster uses bright words and pictures to persuade.
Then ask the tutor: what would a fairer source about this lotion look like?

activities.title: Where do you sit? Agree or disagree
activities.label: Activity 8: Where do you sit? Agree or disagree
activities.intro: Now say what you think about a perspective. Remember that moving along the line after you hear a good reason is not weakness; it is a sign that you are really thinking. Read the statement below, then place yourself on the line: strongly agree, agree, not sure, disagree, or strongly disagree. The statement is: 'Adverts for health products, like Malaria-Gone Lotion, should not be allowed at the market unless they tell the whole truth.'
steps: Write where you sit on the line, from strongly agree to strongly disagree.
Write two reasons for your choice.
Now write down the strongest reason someone who disagrees with you might give.
After thinking about that other view, has your position moved along the line? Say why or why not.

boxes.title: Remember the three classmates
lines: Idris agreed mostly, but felt sellers should just have to write the truth in big letters, not tiny ones.
Sagal strongly agreed, because her little brother believes adverts completely and could get bitten if he trusts the lotion alone.
Faisal disagreed, saying people should learn to check adverts themselves, and sellers have a right to try to sell things.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor where you sit on the line and your two reasons.
Ask it to argue the opposite view as strongly as it can.
Then tell the tutor whether that moved you, and explain why you did or did not change your mind.

activities.title: Use your sources to explain what you think
activities.label: Activity 9: Use your sources to explain what you think
activities.intro: Evaluation leads somewhere: to a clear message you can share, backed by good reasons. Use your strongest sources to explain what you now think about your topic. A clear message does not have to be big. A short, honest point that your sources clearly support is far more convincing than a big claim with nothing behind it.
steps: Write your topic in one sentence.
Write one clear message you would like to share, starting with 'I think ...'.
Choose your two strongest sources.
For each source, write one sentence saying how it supports your message.

boxes.title: A model: Hodan explains what she thinks
lines: Topic: whether Malaria-Gone Lotion is enough protection on its own.
Message: I think families should keep sleeping under a treated net every night, and only use the lotion as extra help outdoors.
Source 1, the clinic leaflet: it shows a treated net is the best protection, backed by a nurse who knows the subject.
Source 2, the fact sheet: it shows mosquitoes are most active at night, exactly when a net protects you and a rubbed-on lotion may have worn off.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your topic, your message and your two supporting sources to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your sources really support your message, or only partly.
Then ask the tutor to help you make your reasons clearer and fairer.

activities.title: Write your own evaluation of a source
activities.label: Activity 10: Write your own evaluation of a source
activities.intro: This is the big one, where every skill comes together. Choose one source about your topic and write a short evaluation of it, using the five-step frame from the Lesson file. Aim for one short paragraph, and do not rush it, because this single paragraph shows off almost everything you have learned in the whole unit.
steps: Who made it? Name the author and what they know.
What is it for? Give the purpose and the perspective.
Pick one clear point the source makes.
Comment on that point: what are its strengths and limitations?
Give your view: do you agree or disagree with the point, and why?

boxes.title: A model evaluation, to guide you
lines: Who made it: a market seller, whose job is to sell the lotion.
What it is for: to make people want to buy it; its perspective is that the lotion alone is enough protection.
A point: the poster says one rub means mosquitoes never bite you again.
Comment: a strength is that it is eye-catching and easy to notice; a limitation is that it never mentions how long the lotion lasts, or the mosquito net at all.
My view: I disagree that the lotion alone is enough, because the clinic leaflet and the fact sheet both say a treated net is the best protection, and the poster does not mention that at all.
When you finish, read your evaluation aloud. A strong evaluation is fair, names both strengths and limitations, and always gives a reason for your view.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your finished evaluation to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you named both a strength and a limitation, and gave a clear reason.
Then ask the tutor to suggest one way to make your evaluation even fairer.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 13 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and use your own words.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'evaluation' mean?
practice.answer: Evaluation means looking carefully at a source and deciding how much you can trust it and how useful it is. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: The two big questions you ask about every source are 'who?' and '______?'.
practice.answer: Why? (You ask 'who made it?' and 'why did they make it?'.)

practice.prompt: The reason a source was made is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its purpose.

practice.prompt: The things a source is good at are its strengths. The things it is not good at are its ______.
practice.answer: Its limitations.

practice.prompt: The person or group who made a source is called the ______.
practice.answer: The author (or creator).

practice.prompt: Is this a fact or an opinion? 'A treated mosquito net stops most mosquitoes from biting you at night.'
practice.answer: A fact. A health worker could check it.

practice.prompt: Is this a fact or an opinion? 'Malaria-Gone Lotion is the best protection you can buy.'
practice.answer: An opinion. Someone could reasonably disagree.

practice.prompt: The point of view a source has is called its ______.
practice.answer: Its perspective.

practice.prompt: Name the three tests you use to decide how far to trust a source.
practice.answer: Expertise, relevance and bias.

practice.prompt: A source that leans unfairly to one side is said to have ______.
practice.answer: Bias.

practice.prompt: True or false: a source is either useful or useless, no matter what your goal is.
practice.answer: False. A source is useful, or not, for a particular goal; it can be great for one job and poor for another.

practice.prompt: Name the five places on the agree and disagree line, from one end to the other.
practice.answer: Strongly agree, agree, not sure, disagree, strongly disagree.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why a source with no author should make you careful.
practice.answer: Any one of: you cannot tell who made it or whether they know the topic; you cannot be sure why it was made; so you cannot be sure it is fair.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each evaluation word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Purpose
options: A. The point of view a source has, shaped by who made it.
B. The reason a source was made; what it is for.
C. The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.
D. The facts or proof that show whether something is true.
E. When a source leans unfairly to one side.
F. The things a source is good at, or does well.
practice.answer: B — The reason a source was made; what it is for.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Perspective
practice.answer: A — The point of view a source has, shaped by who made it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Strengths
practice.answer: F — The things a source is good at, or does well.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Limitations
practice.answer: C — The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Bias
practice.answer: E — When a source leans unfairly to one side.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: D — The facts or proof that show whether something is true.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Sagal finds a voice message about the vaccination day with no name and no date. Should she trust it fully? Explain, using the word author.
practice.answer: No. With no author, Sagal cannot tell who made it or whether they know about vaccinations, so she cannot be sure it is fair. She should find a source with a named, expert author, such as the health clinic.

practice.prompt: Faisal has an advert for 'easy money' phone deals, and a report from a consumer group about phone scams. Which should he trust more, and why?
practice.answer: The consumer group's report, because it comes from a group whose job is to check such deals fairly, while the advert is biased, as the company wants people to sign up.

practice.prompt: Hodan reads that Malaria-Gone Lotion is 'trusted by families everywhere'. Is that a fact or an opinion, and how do you know?
practice.answer: An opinion, because 'trusted by families everywhere' is what the seller wants people to believe, and it cannot be checked or proved; others could disagree.

practice.prompt: Idris wants to persuade drivers to slow down near school. He has one fact about accidents and one strong opinion. Why is it better to use both together?
practice.answer: The fact gives a solid reason, and the opinion says what to do about it. A fact alone does not tell people to act, and an opinion alone is not seen as good proof, so together they persuade best.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour about a market advert or a claim I heard ...
Writing my ideas down in my notebook as I went ...

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what a source is, and who might have made it.
I can say what the purpose of a source is.
I can tell a fact from an opinion in a source.
I can name a strength and a limitation of a source.
I can think about who made a source, and why.
I can say how useful a source is for my goal.
I can identify the perspective of a source.
I can give my opinion about a source, with a reason.
I can discuss a source, considering its author, purpose, strengths and limitations.
I can write my own evaluation of a source.

vocabulary.meaning: Anywhere your information comes from: a person, leaflet, poster, website or message.
The person or group who made a source; also called the creator.
The reason a source was made; what it is for.
The things a source is good at, or does well.
The things a source is not good at, or cannot tell you.
Something that can be checked and shown to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
The point of view a source has, shaped by who made it.
You can believe it, because it is fair and made by someone who knows.
Real knowledge of a topic, which makes a source more trustworthy.
How closely a source is really about your question.
When a source leans unfairly to one side, often because the maker gains.
Deciding how useful and trustworthy a source is for a purpose.
To try to make people agree, or do or buy something.
To give people facts and help them understand.
The facts or proof that show whether something is true.
To give good reasons for a choice or a view.
It helps you with the question or the job you are working on.
The reasons someone gives to try to convince you of something.
A line of choices, such as from strongly agree to strongly disagree.

mistakes: Calling a source simply 'good' or 'bad' instead of asking 'useful for what?'.
Trusting a source just because it looks bright, or comes first in a list.
Forgetting to check who made a source, and why.
Believing an advert as if it were a fair source of facts.
Naming only strengths, or only limitations, instead of both.
Mixing up a fact with an opinion.
Agreeing or disagreeing without giving a reason.
